topic: understanding the concept of a system of equations with no solution or infinite solutions

easy.text: Two lines are parallel (never intersect). How many solutions does this system of equations have?

options.feedback: Correct -- since parallel lines never cross, there's no point that satisfies both equations at once.
One solution would require the lines to intersect at exactly one point, but parallel lines never intersect at all.
Infinite solutions would require the lines to be identical (overlapping), not simply parallel and separate.
Two straight lines can share at most one intersection point (or be identical/parallel) -- "exactly two" isn't a possible outcome here.

medium.text: Two equations, when simplified, turn out to be exactly identical (like y=2x+3 and 2y=4x+6). How many solutions does this system have?

options.feedback: Correct -- since both equations describe the exact same line, every point on that line satisfies both equations.
This would apply to parallel, non-identical lines -- identical lines actually share ALL their points in common, giving infinite solutions.
One solution would apply to two distinct lines crossing at a single point -- identical lines share every point, not just one.
This case can definitely be determined -- identical equations always represent the same line, giving infinitely many shared solutions.

hard.text: A system of equations is: 2x + 3y = 6 and 4x + 6y = 15. Without fully solving, how can you tell this system has no solution?

options.text: Multiplying the first equation by 2 gives 4x+6y=12, but the second equation says 4x+6y=15 -- the left sides match but the right sides don't
options.feedback: Correct -- since the left sides match but the right sides don't, the lines are parallel and distinct, meaning no solution exists.

options.text: This system definitely has exactly one solution
options.feedback: This isn't correct -- checking the coefficient pattern reveals these lines are actually parallel (matching left sides, mismatched right sides), meaning no solution exists.

options.text: This system has infinitely many solutions
options.feedback: This isn't correct -- infinite solutions would require the equations to be fully identical (including the right side), but here the right sides don't match up correctly.

options.text: There is no way to determine this without graphing both lines first
options.feedback: This CAN be determined algebraically by comparing coefficient ratios, without necessarily needing to graph the lines first.

easy.hard: Consider the geometric relationship between two lines that maintain a constant separation and never meet.
easy.medium: Think about what it means for two lines to never touch each other.
easy.easy: Parallel lines never cross, so there's no shared point.

medium.hard: Consider what it means geometrically for two equations to describe exactly the same line.
medium.medium: If the equations describe the exact same line, then every single point on that line works for both.
medium.easy: If both equations describe the exact same line, every point on it counts as a solution.

hard.hard: Compare the ratio of coefficients on the left side of each equation to the ratio of the constant terms -- if the coefficient ratios match but the constant ratio doesn't, the lines are parallel and distinct.
hard.medium: Try multiplying the first equation by a constant to match the second equation's left side, then compare the right sides to see if they also match up.
hard.easy: Multiply the first equation by 2 to get 4x+6y=12, then compare that to the actual second equation's 15 -- they don't match, so no solution exists.
